prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 1e-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved from B002 to B018, and the reason is scientific as well as a matter of what the discussion exposed. The magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition while holding very many atoms in a regime free of Doppler and recoil broadening, which is what separates it from single-ion clocks that reach low uncertainty by a different route and with far fewer atoms. The result is measured, not inferred, with uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, reproduced and compared in independent laboratories, and it already feeds tests of constant variation, ultralight dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, with Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for carrying the clock to record accuracy and many-body-limited operation. No colleague disputes its maturity or originality, and the chair's summary shows that its critics (Pearce, Johansson and I) attack timing or discovery character, not the science. I could not answer the questions put to me about B002 (which single result carries the citation, and who is least dispensable among four people for three places), and that matters more to me than the fact that I was alone on it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation about B018 is that it can be read as a refinement built on laser cooling (1997), the optical frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012), and that it is metrology rather than the opening of a new phenomenon or messenger. I think the magic-wavelength step is separable from those, but the committee should word the citation narrowly on lattice clocks so that it does not imply credit for optical clocks in general. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and I have not verified the priority sequence between the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks. The redefinition of the second is still pending. Against my former choice, B002 remains conceptually strong but suffers from crowded credit (Crooks), contested priority for the steady-state relation, and the fact that its experimental confirmations test exact identities more than they reveal a new phenomenon.

responses.point: Kroll holds B018 first and names the overlap with cooling, combs and ion clocks as his strongest reservation, but judges that the magic-wavelength idea is a new concept that changes what is possible.
responses.response: This is the point I pressed in round 1 and I now think your reading is the better one. Cooling and the comb are tools used in the lattice clock, but they do not produce the cancellation of the light shift, and ion clocks do not provide the large atom number that gives the stability. That makes the lattice step separable in physics, not only in credit. I would still ask that the citation says magic-wavelength lattice clocks, not optical clocks, so that the ion-clock lineage is not implied to be covered or excluded by accident. Your remark that a single-part, two-person prize is a complete configuration persuaded me not to look for a second part.

responses.point: Danielsson distinguishes a discovery measured in nature from exact identities, finds B002's attribution arbitrary at three names, and says he would move if the experimental verification gave B002 more of a discovery character.
responses.response: You and I disagree less than my first-round ranking suggested. The tweezer, RNA-unfolding and colloid experiments are real confirmations, but they confirm relations that are mathematical consequences of the dynamics, so I accept your distinction and cannot claim a new measured phenomenon. On the attribution I concede that I could not defend a three-name cut against Crooks, and the Evans priority is contested. I therefore do not argue for B002 against B018 and keep it only as an alternative. On your worry that the four first places reflect a shared taste for instruments, I am a theorist from a different field and I reach B018 anyway.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B007 first, with Halzen and Karle for the conception and construction of IceCube and the diffuse flux, and finds a three-name credit dilutes the instrumentation story.
responses.response: I accept your objection to three names and I withdraw the suggestion of Yoshida as a repair; it does not solve the attribution problem, it moves it. The discovery of the diffuse flux is secure, and the chair's question whether a new observational window should outrank a precision advance is the real issue. My answer is that a new window is the stronger discovery in the abstract, but this committee has to award names, and I cannot see which two or three people the 2013 evidence singles out within a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and Baikal precursors. I would not oppose B007 if the committee found a defensible credit, which is why I keep it in mind, but I rank it below B018 on present evidence and I do not list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B020 to B018 after reading the ballots, asked me which of the three steps carries the B002 citation, and noted that Crooks makes the allocation no cleaner than for topological insulators.
responses.response: Your question has no clean answer from me, and that is part of why I moved. If forced, the Jarzynski equality is the most portable single result and Seifert's trajectory-level entropy production the most systematic, but then the steady-state relation and Crooks's detailed theorem are both left out, and a citation for a family of relations is harder to make accurate. Our two moves are for different reasons, you partly on the vote and I on the credit problem. I would rather say plainly that my own B002 has the same weakness that I attributed to B020 and B034, so I cannot hold B018's critics to a standard that my own candidate fails.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B018 for the magic-wavelength lattice, notes that her priority account is from recollection, and asks whether the committee wants discovery-level physics or a broader optical-clock citation.
responses.response: I agree on the narrow citation and I share the caveat about recollection: nothing in the material before me verifies who proposed the lattice first, and I would not want the citation to settle a priority question the committee cannot document. On the timing, I think the pending redefinition is a consequence of the clocks and not a condition for recognising them; the 1e-18 performance is established whether or not the second is redefined this year.

responses.point: Johansson keeps B032 first (Cirac and Zoller) and argues the 2012 prize recognised the experiments, not the proposals, while conceding that B018 is better supported.
responses.response: The separation you draw between 2012 and the proposals is fair and I overstated the overlap in round 1. My remaining difficulty is the one you raise yourself, that B032 and B015 share Cirac and Zoller, so a prize on one affects the other, and with a three-person limit I cannot see how Bloch and Greiner would be handled. That is a structural problem for the committee, not a defect in the science, and it keeps B032 below B018 for me this year.

uncertainties: Whether the priority between the early lattice proposals and the first operating lattice clocks supports crediting Katori and Ye alone, which I have not verified and which several colleagues also flag.
Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as a refinement of the 1997, 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the citation wording can express that distinction.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay a prize, which I think it should not.
Whether a defensible two- or three-name credit for IceCube exists, which would reopen the choice between a new observational window and a precision advance.
Whether the experimental credit for B044 can be limited fairly while the superconducting mechanism is unsettled; this is why I do not lead with it.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye, or to any other credited name on the shortlist, appears in my documented record of co-authors, supervisors or institutions. My research on stochastic processes is intellectually close to stochastic thermodynamics (B002). That was a possible bias in round 1, and I have now moved away from B002, so it no longer bears on my preferred configuration, but I will not argue for B002 as an alternative with more weight than the evidence gives it. My field is not metrology, and I rely on Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson for the technical claims about lattice-clock systematics.
